strengths: Proposes a genuinely novel architectural adaptation of Mixture-of-Transformers for 3D generation, decoupling token-level (TokenAR) and block-level (BlockAR) modeling with a shared causal-parallel attention mechanism, which is a reasonable and well-motivated solution to the sequence-length bottleneck of prior LLM-based 3D mesh/token generation.

Effectively reuses a pretrained vision-language backbone (Qwen3-VL) and a frozen 3D VAE (Hunyuan3D-2.1), reducing training cost while inheriting strong 2D understanding priors -- this is a practical and scalable design choice.

Comprehensive empirical study: quantitative comparison against both MLLM-based and non-MLLM-based 3D generators (Table 1), a 100-person/2400-point user study, 3D captioning benchmarks (Table 2), and five ablation groups covering VAE backbone, MOT necessity, LLM backbone size, token length, and compute scaling (Tables 3-5).

Honest negative-result reporting, including the failure of AdaLN in the multimodal LLM setting and VAE reconstruction artifacts from importance-point sampling, which is valuable for future reproducibility and understanding of design pitfalls.

Demonstrates an interesting bidirectional benefit: joint training for 3D generation improves image-based 3D understanding/captioning relative to the base Qwen3-VL, supporting the paper's core motivating claim about generation-perception synergy.

Clear qualitative results (Figs. 4, 5, 9-12) showing reasonably complete and detailed geometry compared to other MLLM-based baselines (SAR3D, ShapeLLM-Omni), with a forthright limitations/failure-case section (Fig. 8).
weaknesses: The method does not surpass non-MLLM-based SOTA baselines; e.g., TRELLIS achieves p-FID 7.36 and p-KID 0.12 versus the proposed method's 12.55 and 0.27, a substantial gap the paper acknowledges but does not fully address or contextualize with per-category breakdowns.

In the 3D captioning comparison, the model trails specialized 3D-input methods (3D-LLM, PointLLM, ShapeLLM-Omni-7B) by a wide margin, and the chosen 'Image Inputs' baselines (LLaVA-13B, InstructBLIP-13B, Qwen3-VL-2B) are much smaller/general-purpose models not fine-tuned for this task, making the 'consistently better' claim potentially misleading regarding true 3D-understanding capability.

Scalability claims are only lightly tested -- the largest backbone evaluated is Qwen3-VL-2B, and the largest 3D token budget is 4096, both far below the resolution needed to compete with leading 3D generation systems (as the paper itself notes 10x more tokens are typically required), leaving the central 'high-resolution' claim only partially substantiated.

Reproducibility details are thin: exact dataset sizes/splits, hyperparameters for the two training stages beyond learning rate/CFG, and code/model release are not clearly specified, making independent verification difficult.

Some claims in the abstract/introduction (e.g., 'significantly outperforms existing MLLMs') are true only relative to other MLLM-based methods and could be stated more precisely given the acknowledged gap to non-MLLM SOTA.

The captions used for training (typically <20 words per the paper) limit the depth of 3D understanding that can be claimed, yet the introduction and contributions emphasize 'precise spatial understanding' somewhat more strongly than the evidence supports.

The ablation in Table 3 conflates several factors changing simultaneously (VAE, MOT, backbone, token count) in a non-fully-factorial design, making it harder to isolate the individual contribution of each component with confidence.

strengths: The paper tackles a genuinely underexplored problem: natively integrating high-resolution 3D generation into an MLLM rather than relying on an external diffusion decoder conditioned on LLM semantics.

The TokenAR/BlockAR dual-transformer design with a shared causal-parallel attention mask is a reasonably creative adaptation of Mixture-of-Transformers to mix serial text/image tokens with parallel 3D block tokens, and the paper provides some architectural detail (masking patterns, positional encoding treatment for permutation invariance of 3D blocks).

The authors report several negative/engineering findings (AdaLN instability in the MLLM context, VAE reconstruction holes from importance-point sampling) that could be useful to practitioners, and these are presented honestly rather than hidden.

Reasonably broad set of ablations (VAE backbone, MOT vs. non-MOT, LLM backbone size, token budget, compute/memory scaling) and a stated limitations section that acknowledges failure cases and the remaining gap to non-MLLM SOTA.
weaknesses: Central claims are overstated relative to the evidence: the abstract/intro claim CG-MLLM achieves 'high-fidelity' and 'high-resolution' 3D generation 'bringing 3D creation into the mainstream LLM paradigm,' yet Table 1 shows the method is worse than several non-MLLM baselines (e.g., TRELLIS has p-FID 7.36/p-KID 0.12 vs. the proposed method's 12.55/0.27, and Hunyuan3D-2.1 has higher CLIP). The 'state-of-the-art' claim is only true within the narrow MLLM-based subset, which is not made sufficiently prominent in the abstract/contributions.

The claim that '3D generation transfers back to perception' is supported by an apples-to-oranges comparison: the method is only compared against image-only baselines (LLaVA, InstructBLIP, Qwen3-VL) that never see 3D/point-cloud input, while the method itself trails point-cloud/3D-latent-input baselines (3D-LLM, PointLLM, ShapeLLM-Omni-7B) in Table 2. No controlled ablation isolates whether the captioning gains come from joint generation training versus simply additional fine-tuning/data, undermining the causal claim made in the abstract and contributions list.

Reproducibility is weak: no code/data/checkpoint release is mentioned, several architectural details (exact parameter sharing between TokenAR/BlockAR, how 'Shared Causal-Parallel Self-Attention' is implemented at the weight level, the full training data composition/sizes, exact user-study protocol/questions/rater demographics) are not specified in sufficient detail to reproduce the system.

The quantitative ablation in Table 3 changes multiple factors simultaneously across rows (VAE, MOT, backbone, token count), making it difficult to cleanly attribute performance gains to any single design choice; the claimed 'scaling-law trend' is asserted from only two backbone sizes (0.5B vs 2B), which is a very thin basis for such a claim.

Despite being framed as efficient, Table 5 shows inference time scaling roughly quadratically with 3D-token count (12s→45s from 512 to 5120 tokens) and the method still caps out at under 4096 tokens, an order of magnitude lower than 'current high-resolution 3D generation methods' as the authors themselves admit in the Limitations section — this is in tension with the title's claim of 'high-resolution 3D generation.'

The Impact Statement is perfunctory ('none of which we feel must be specifically highlighted'), despite the paper using large-scale scraped 3D asset datasets (Objaverse++, Trellis-500K) with associated copyright/licensing and misuse considerations for 3D asset generation that merit at least brief discussion.

Qualitative comparisons (Fig. 4, 5) and the user study appear selectively curated without clear sampling protocol, and no standard deviation/significance testing is reported for the quantitative metrics in Table 1-3, making it hard to assess whether reported improvements over MLLM baselines are statistically meaningful.

strengths: Addresses a genuine gap: most existing 3D-capable MLLMs rely on coarse voxel/lego proxies or token-limited mesh text and offload fine detail to an external diffusion model; CG-MLLM attempts true end-to-end high-resolution generation within a single LLM-centric architecture.

The Mixture-of-Transformers adaptation (TokenAR for sequential tokens, BlockAR for parallel 3D blocks) bound by generation-mode rather than task is a reasonable architectural idea, and the ablation (Table 3, rows 2-3) shows a sizeable gain from adding the MOT design (p-FID 44.91→30.60) isolated from VAE/backbone changes.

Practical engineering insight is shared transparently: the AdaLN instability finding (Sec 4.3) and the VAE point-sampling/importance-point reconstruction artifact (Sec 4.4) are useful negative results for the community, going beyond a typical 'things that worked' paper.

Reasonably broad empirical study: comparisons against both non-MLLM (Michelangelo, CraftsMan, Hunyuan3D-2.1, TRELLIS, SAM3D) and MLLM-based (SAR3D, ShapeLLM-Omni) baselines, plus a captioning/understanding evaluation and a user study, plus scaling/cost tables (Tab 4-5).

Interesting and plausible finding that joint training for 3D generation improves image-based 3D understanding relative to the base Qwen3-VL, suggesting generation and perception are mutually reinforcing in this framework.
Honest limitations and failure-case discussion (ambiguous inputs, semantic hallucination, gap to commercial systems, VAE token-budget ceiling) rather than only showcasing successes.
weaknesses: The quantitative gains over compared MLLM-based methods, while present, are not uniformly large, and the paper explicitly concedes it does not surpass non-MLLM SOTA (e.g., TRELLIS has notably better p-FID/p-KID); the abstract's claim of 'significantly outperforms existing MLLMs' is stronger than what Table 1 actually shows (CLIP-IQA+ and CLIP are only tied or second-best).

In the captioning/understanding comparison (Table 2), the method underperforms 3D-latent-input specialist models (3D-LLM, PointLLM, ShapeLLM-Omni-7B) and is only compared favorably against image-input baselines, a comparison that is not fully apples-to-apples given different input modalities and dataset scale differences the authors themselves note.

The user study is underspecified: no description of rater recruitment, instructions, inter-rater agreement, or statistical significance testing for the '100 questionnaires / ~2400 data points' claim, limiting confidence in this result.

Reproducibility is a concern: no mention of code, model weights, or public dataset release; many architectural and training details (exact MoT masking implementation, exact data splits/sizes per source, hyperparameter sensitivity) are only partially specified, which would make independent replication difficult.

Figure 4's qualitative comparison includes crossed-out (⊘) results for some baselines without any explanation in the text of why those entries are omitted/failed, reducing the transparency and fairness of the qualitative comparison.

The ethics/impact statement is essentially boilerplate and does not engage with relevant considerations specific to 3D generative models trained on large scraped 3D asset corpora (e.g., Objaverse data provenance, copyright/licensing of 3D assets, potential misuse for counterfeit physical object replication).

Resolution is capped at 4096 3D tokens, which the authors acknowledge is an order of magnitude below what current high-resolution 3D pipelines use, so the central claim of enabling 'high-resolution 3D content creation' is relative only to prior MLLM-based work and still falls short of production-quality non-MLLM systems.
